suggestions.assertion: The reply has the PM bring the CEO concrete options with explicit trade-offs (for example what drops from the roadmap, a smaller first version, or phased dates) instead of a flat no.
suggestions.reason: All four samples pass this, and A3 (no overtime) and A4 (problem behind the features) too, so they don't separate the samples. A sharper check: the PM recommends one option and says why instead of only laying out a menu. B and C do this ('recommend an option and ask him to choose'; 'Say which one you recommend and why'); A and D don't.

suggestions.assertion: The reply has the PM size the three features against the team's real capacity before answering, rather than accepting or refusing outright.
suggestions.reason: 'Real capacity' is loose. B estimates the features and maps them onto roadmap slips but takes 'at capacity' as given. A, C and D check what time is actually free (leave, on-call, support, incidents, tech debt). If that is the intent, require the free-capacity check explicitly.

suggestions.assertion: The reply keeps the relationship in mind: private conversation first, assuming pressure rather than bad intent, and suggests agreeing a process so future promises are checked with product first.
suggestions.reason: This bundles three separate behaviours (private first, assume pressure, process for future promises). All four samples meet all three, but splitting them would make failures easier to diagnose.

No assertion checks whether the PM separates product work from a one-customer custom build (A and D do: 'maintained forever'), or brings their own manager or engineering lead in before facing the CEO alone (all four do). Both are useful advice that the assertions don't reward.

eval_feedback.overall: Strong, complete advice with a ready-to-send note and a clear options table, but at 808 words it is far too long to act on quickly.
